comparison: Both evaluate SFOAE measurements (C16-C23) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes methodological details, sample size, and statistical rigor. Peer reviewers describe the OAE data as 'solid,' 'believable,' and 'novel' with no concerns raised. Strong agreement on data quality.

Both evaluate auditory-nerve measurements (C24-C28) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights adequate sample size and statistical testing. Peer reviewers describe the data as 'solid,' 'believable,' and showing 'fairly normal-looking cochlear tuning.' Complete agreement on data quality.

Both address tuning ratio calculations (C29-C37, C49-C50) but with different emphases. OpenEval finds claims SUPPORTED despite acknowledging extrapolation uncertainty. Peer reviewers mark as UNCERTAIN, specifically noting that extrapolation of chicken data 'in the most interesting regions (beyond 3.5 kHz)' is a key limitation. Disagreement on confidence level.

Both address SFOAE predictions matching auditory-nerve data (C38-C40, C43-C44). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with close agreement shown in Figure 5. Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED, noting 'quite good correspondence' and 'significant support for the utility of otoacoustic estimates.' Strong agreement.

Both evaluate behavioral literature summary (C9-C15, C51-C52). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as accurate summaries of prior work. Peer reviewers mark as UNCERTAIN, expressing concern that 'comparisons are between studies separated by decades' and that 'the reason for the discrepant behavioral results remains unexplained.' Disagreement on interpretation confidence.

Both address main conclusions comparing SFOAE, auditory-nerve, and behavioral measures (C40-C41, C53, C64-C66). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with logical inference from data convergence. Peer reviewers mark as UNCERTAIN due to reliance on chicken data extrapolation in critical 3.5-4 kHz range. Disagreement on conclusion certainty.

OpenEval R6 addresses main conclusions (C64-C66) while Peer R10 addresses the same claims. Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers affirm findings are 'important' and provide 'significant support,' stating differences are 'likely more central in origin.' Agreement on overall conclusions.

Perfect match on behavioral paradigm discussion (C54-C59). Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate citations and reasonable speculation about central processing. Peer reviewers accept interpretation that findings 'imply that any behavioral/perceptual differences are likely more central in origin.' Complete agreement.

Perfect match on prior literature citations (C60-C61). Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes these provide supporting evidence from literature. Peer reviewers do not challenge these claims, accepting consistency with current results. Complete agreement.

Both address background and context claims (C1-C8). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting appropriate citations establishing study rationale. Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED, accepting motivation and established relationships from prior literature. Strong agreement.

Both address comparative findings and tuning ratio framework (C29-C31, C42, C45-C48). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate qualifications. Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED, explicitly noting acceptance of tuning ratio concept and its application. Agreement on framework validity.

Both address limitations of chicken data (C49-C50). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting authors appropriately acknowledge extrapolation limitation. Peer reviewers mark as UNCERTAIN, emphasizing that extrapolation in critical frequency regions is a significant limitation. Disagreement on severity of limitation.

Both evaluate statistical methods and methodological details (C71, C85-C90 and broader methods C67-C84). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with appropriate statistical approach. Peer reviewers implicitly support methods by describing resulting data as 'solid' and 'believable' with no methodological concerns. Agreement on methods adequacy.
